list.listitem: Acute myelogenous leukemia (AML) is the most common form of acute leukemia in adults. Patients present with insidious symptoms related to variable degrees of bone marrow failure. C
The diagnosis of AML is demonstrated by increased number of myeloblasts (>20%) in the bone marrow or the peripheral blood. B

The cornerstone of treatment is chemotherapy given in two phases: induction and consolidation. Bone marrow transplantation and investigational drugs such as FLT3 inhibitors may be used in selected patients with relapsed or refractory disease.B
Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) has distinctive clinical and morphologic features, and its treatment is based on all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA). It carries a better overall prognosis. B
Despite recent molecular and therapeutic advance, overall prognosis of AML patients remains poor. C

background.definition: Acute myelogenous leukemias (AML, also called acute myelocytic leukemia or acute myeloid leukemia) are clonal malignant hematopoietic disorders resulting from genetic alterations in normal hematopoietic stem cells. These alterations induce differentiation arrest and/or excessive proliferation of abnormal leukemic cells or blasts deriving from myeloid stem cell line. Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a distinct subtype of AML that constitutes 8% to 10% of AMLs. It has particular clinical, molecular, and therapeutic features. It is characterized by the translocation t(15;17) involving the retinoic acid receptor-alpha (RAR-alpha), which is present in 95% of APLs.

list.listitem: The incidence of AML is 5.5 per 100,000 persons per year.
The incidence of AML increases with age, and the median age at presentation is about 65 years.
In adults, AML is by far the most common type of acute leukemia.
An increased incidence of AML is seen in patients with disorders associated with excessive chromatin fragility such as Bloom's syndrome, Fanconi's anemia, and Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
Patients with chromosomal abnormalities like Down (trisomy of chromosome 21), Klinefelter (XXY and variants), and Patau (trisomy of chromosome 13) syndromes have a higher incidence of AML.
Therapeutic radiation increases AML risk, particularly if given with alkylating agents. Survivors of the atomic bombs in Japan had an increased incidence of AML.
Drugs such as chloramphenicol, phenylbutazone, chloroquine, and methoxypsoralen can induce marrow damage that may later evolve into AML.
AML following exposure to benzene, smoking, dyes, herbicides, and pesticides has also been described.
AML may also be secondary to an antecedent hematologic disorder, such as polycythemia vera, chronic myelogenous leukemia, primary thrombocytosis, or paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.

In AML, the process of cell differentiation during hematopoiesis is interrupted in the cells of myeloid lineage. Excessive proliferation of these cells can lead to a clonal disorder. Several chromosomal abnormalities and mutations have been identified:

The t(8;21), t(16;16), and inv(16) mutations are associated with a better prognosis, whereas alterations of 11q23, leading to the mixed-lineage leukemia rearrangement, portends a worse outcome. The mutation in FLT3 (tyrosine kinase receptor) is the most common one in AML and is associated with poor clinical outcome.
t(15;17) is always associated with APL, and leads to a mutation in the RAR implicated in hematopoietic differentiation.

Patients with AML usually present with nonspecific symptoms, mostly related to infections and bleeding. Other signs include organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and soft tissue and meningeal infiltration (more common with monocytic variants, M4 or M5). C
The diagnosis of AML is demonstrated by increased number of myeloblasts (>20%) in the bone marrow or peripheral blood. B

Flow cytometry is necessary to differentiate between myloid and lymphoid leukemic cells. Cytogenetic studies carry prognostic and therapeutic implications, and are mandatory prior to treatment initiation. C
Tumor lysis syndrome (common in APL) and leukostasis are oncologic emergencies and require prompt recognition and management. C

list.listitem: Most patients present initially with nonspecific symptoms: viral-like illness, malaise, fatigue symptoms, fever, easy bruising, or bleeding. Anorexia is common, but weight loss is unusual. Diffuse bone tenderness is the initial manifestation in 25% of the patients.

The most common physical finding are bleeding and infection in different organs. Splenomegaly is present in 50% of patients. Lymphadenopathy is rare and is present in less than 10% of patients. Infiltration of gingivae, skin, soft tissues, or meninges is most commonly seen in monocytic subgroups.
Disseminated intravascular coagulopathy (DIC) with bleeding diathesis is a common presentation in APL.
Skin involvement, or leukemia cutis, is present in 10% of patients.
Only 10% of patients present with WBC counts greater than 100 x 109/L. These patients are at higher risk of tumor lysis syndrome, CNS involvement, and leukostasis.

Leukostasis and tumor lysis syndrome are oncologic emergencies and require prompt recognition and management. Leukostasis may manifest as dyspnea, chest pain, headaches, altered mental status, cranial nerve palsies, or priapism. Tumor lysis syndrome is characterized by hyperuricemia, renal failure, acidosis, hypocalcemia, and hyperphosphatemia.
Bone marrow aspirate is necessary for the diagnosis of AML unless the peripheral blast count is high. Order bone marrow biopsy if aspirate cannot be obtained.

By the French-American-British (FAB) Cooperative Group criteria, acute leukemia is diagnosed when a 200-cell differential reveals the presence of 30% or more blasts in a marrow aspirate. The minimal criterion has recently been changed to 20% by the World Health Organization (WHO). Patients with the cytogenetic abnormalities t(8;21)(q22;q22), inversion(16)(p13q22) or t(16;16)(p13;q22), and t(15;17)(q22;q12) should be considered to have AML regardless of the blast percentage.

After establishing the diagnosis of acute leukemia, the blast lineage (myeloid, lymphoid, or undifferentiated) is determined using cytochemical stains. With the exception of the presence of Auer rods, which specifically indicates a myeloid origin, none of the other morphologic features are reliable to distinguish myeloblasts from lymphoblasts. For this reason, immunophenotyping are essential in the diagnosis of AML. Cytochemistry can be omitted if four-color cytometry is available.

Cytogenetics are essential: reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) further classifies acute leukemias into APL and non-APL subgroups. A sedimentation rate >100 mm/h is specific but not sensitive (25%). A sedimentation rate of less than 100 does not significantly reduce risk of malignancy.
Suspect AML in patients experiencing unexplained constitutional symptoms and signs of bone marrow involvement, including recurrent infections and bleeding.

Initial evaluation should include CBC with peripheral blood smear and bone marrow aspiration (or biopsy). The diagnosis of AML is confirmed by increased number of myeloblasts (>20%) in the bone marrow or the peripheral blood.
The subgroup of AML is defined further by cytogenetic, immunophenotypic, and cytometric studies. The therapeutic approach is summarized in

Conventional treatment for AML is divided into remission induction therapy and postremission therapy. Induction combines an anthracycline with cytarabine. Maintenance therapy is based on the same drugs given in cycles (see ). B
In acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL), add all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) to an anthracycline during induction. ATRA is also used in postremission therapy. B
Stem cell transplantation may be offered to patients in chronic remission, especially younger patients and those with bad prognostic karyotypes. C
In patients with relapsed or refractory AML and the FLT3 mutation, gliteritinib increased overall survival and the likelihood of remission. Other targetted therapies are being developed. B
Individualize treatment of older AML patients depending on specific comorbidity factors. C

Conventional treatment for AML is divided into remission induction therapy and postremission therapy. Induction therapy combines an anthracycline (ie, idarubicin, daunorubicin), given daily for 3 days, with an antimetabolite, cytarabine, given at 100 to 200 mg/m2 daily for 7 days by continuous infusion (3+7 regimen).

Typically, once in remission after treatment with the 3+7 regimen, patients receive maintenance therapy, with the same drugs given during induction administered at approximately monthly intervals for 4 to 12 months.

Idarubicin has been proposed as the anthracycline of choice; other anthracyclines, ie, mitoxantrone or daunorubicin, may be used with comparable results. A systematic review found that idarubicin had a lower remission failure rate than daunorubicin (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.66-0.99), but there was no difference in all-cause mortality. The benefit was only seen in studies with a daunorubicin to idarubicin dose ratio less than 5.
In patients younger than 65 and those who carry good-prognosis carytoypes, high-dose cytarabine (ara-C, HDAC; 1-3 g/m2) can be used, with better relapse-free and event-free survival (see ).

A randomized trial in adults 15 to 55 years with AML randomized 591 to intermediate dose or high dose cytarabine along with daunorubicin and omacetaxine mepesuccinate. Three year disease free survival was higher in the intermediate dose group (67% vs 54%, p = 0.005, NNT = 8). Three year overall survival was also higher (68% vs 59%, p = 0.014, NNT = 11).

Treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is distinct. Add all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) to an anthracycline during induction. ATRA is also used in postremission therapy for APL. Treat the coagulopathy to keep the platelets greater than 50 x 109/L together with fresh-frozen plasma and cryoprecipitate to normalize the activated partial thromboplastin time and fibrinogen levels.

High-dose chemotherapy with or without radiation followed by hematopoietic cell transplantation is increasingly used as therapy for AML in first complete remission, particularly in patients with poor-risk factors such as deletion of 5q and 7q, trisomy 8, t(6;9), t(9;22), and a history of myelodysplasia.
Younger patients (<20 years old) may have better results with transplant compared with induction chemotherapy.
Elderly transplanted AML patients have a high mortality, which excludes the use of conventional myeloablative therapy.
The combination of ATRA, arsenic trioxide, and gentuzumab ozogamycin (Mylotarg) has also been used in induction and maintenance therapy in APL with promising results.

Gentuzumab ozogamycin (Mylotarg), a conjugate composed of a humanized anti-CD33 antibody linked to the antitumor antibiotic calicheamicin, is the only approved treatment for relapsed AML in patients older than 60 with CRD1 1st complete remission duration of 3 months or longer.
Sorafenib may have activity in AML, but its use is investigational with only case reports at this time.

A trial identified 371 patients with relapsed or refractory AML carrying the FLT3-mutation and randomized them to gilteritinib (a selective FLT3 inhibitor) or salvage chemotherapy. Complete remission was more likely in the gilteritinib group (34% vs 15%, p < 0.05, NNT = 5) as was overall survival (9.3 vs 5.6 months, p < 0.001), with fewer adverse events.

A study of 472 patients who had gone through induction therapy and were in remission randomized them to the oral version of the hypomethylating agent azacitidine (CC-486) or placebo. Overall survival was longer with CC-486, 24.7 months vesus 14.8 months, p < 0.001.

Researchers identified 146 patients with newly diagnosed IDH1- mutated acute myeloid leukemia who were not eligible for intensive induction chemotherapy. They were randomized to ivosidenib + andazacitidine or placebo + andazacitidine. Median overall survival was significantly longer with combination therapy (24 vs 8 months, p < 0.001); harms included higher rates of bleeding and neutropenia.
Adequate and close supportive care is extremely important in the care of acute leukemia.

Both granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) and granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) have reduced the median time to neutrophil recovery by an average of 5 to 7 days. Thus, their use can be considered after consolidation therapy, and after induction therapy if suspected risk of neutropenia exceeds 40%. However, a systematic review of 19 studies with over 5000 patients of all risk levels found no reduction in all-cause mortality, bacteremia rates, remission rates, relapse-free survival rates or rates of invasive fungal infection with use of GM-CSF compared to placebo, though. Their use does appear to be safe.

Give platelet transfusions as needed to maintain a platelet count above 10 x 109/L. A trial comparing a no transfusion strategy with routine transfusionin patients with hematologic cancer found more clinically significant bleeds in the no transfusion group.
Administer RBC transfusions to keep the hemoglobin level above 8 g/dL in the absence of active bleeding, DIC, symptoms at rest, or cardiopulmonary disease.
Prevention of tumor lysis syndrome is required on administration of IV fluid hydration, and allopurinol (or rasburicase) if the blast count is above 10 x 109 cells/L.

While antibiotic prophylaxis is controversial, development of fever (>101A F/38.3A C) in neutropenic patients calls for administration of broad-spectrum antibiotics, such as imipenem or a third- (eg, ceftazidime) or fourth-generation cephalosporin (eg, cefepime).

Add vancomycin for patients at risk for Staphylococcus infections (ie, indwelling catheters, portacaths). Antibiotic selection should be prompt, individualized, and in accordance with the updated antibiotic susceptibility profile of each particular institution.
Consider antifungals and antiviral therapy in the presence of persistent fever despite maximized antibiotic coverage.
The diagnosis of AML prompts emergency workup and treatment, as the disease is rapidly fatal if untreated. C
The most important prognostic factors are cytogenetics and age: younger patients (<60) and patients who carry the translocations t(15;17), t(8;21) and inv(16) have better outcomes (see and ). B
The percentage of patients achieving complete remission is 50% to 70%. The overall survival remains poor (25%-30% long-term survival). C

Provide close follow-up of patients receiving treatment for AML during the period of treatment and after therapy. Follow-up should include regular blood tests including CBC and chemistry to monitor the need for transfusion and to assess for possible treatment- or disease-related complications.

Survivors of childhood malignancy are known to be at increased risk of second malignancy, but recent data with 15 year follow-up is encouraging as the risk of second malignancy in this group has declined in recent decades.

AML in older adults is considered a biologically and clinically distinct entity. Leukemic cells in older patients appear to be intrinsically more resistant to standard chemotherapy. The presence of comorbid conditions and decreased marrow reserve contributes to the worse results.

Therefore, individualize treatment depending on prognostic factors. Treatment options include: standard intensive therapy for patients with no adverse factors or at most one adverse factor, and alternative, low-intensity investigational therapies for those with multiple adverse factors. Such therapies include targeted therapies, low-dose Ara-C, nucleoside analogs, hypomethylating agents, and other palliative regimens.
